content: The PICO framework, which stands for Problem, Intervention or Indicator, Comparison, and Outcome of interest, was utilized to guide the development of standards. Two systematic reviews of the literature were commissioned to address the PICO questions. These reviews retrieved evidence from databases containing medical, health, and policy-related publications. The first review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of prosthetics and orthotics services, while the second focused on identifying the skills required to deliver and manage high-quality services, including standards and models. Both review teams included a broad network of reviewers. Representatives from the review teams participated in a consensus meeting of the Standards Development Group in Bangkok, Thailand, in November 2015. During this meeting, they presented their findings, which helped define the scope of the standards and set directions for the document's development. The World Health Organization (WHO) commissioned two authors to draft the document in close collaboration with representatives of the WHO Steering Group. The Standards Development Group reviewed two drafts, selected and ranked the standards, appraised the evidence supporting the standards, provided examples of best practices, and contributed content for specific sections. An External Review Group was also consulted during the second review phase. All consultation responses, including consensus outcomes, expert opinions, and evidence, were incorporated into the final standards and content. The management of conflicts of interest was a critical priority throughout the development process. WHO has stringent policies to avoid conflicts of interest, particularly in the creation of official guidance documents that influence healthcare. All authors and meeting participants were required to declare any potential conflicts of interest. Members of the Standards Development Group and the External Review Group signed the Declaration of Conflict of Interests for WHO Experts. WHO also published the names and brief biographies of the Standards Development Group members on its website for public notice and comment. After analyzing each declaration, it was concluded that no conflicts of interest existed that would exclude any individual from participating in the development process. Two lead authors were selected through the WHO Request for Proposals bidding process. Anders Eklund, a former WHO employee and current freelance consultant, and Sandra Sexton, a former director of the National Centre for Prosthetics and Orthotics at the University of Strathclyde and grant manager for ISPO, served as the lead authors. WHO colleagues involved in the development process were also deemed free of direct conflicts of interest. The 60 standards presented in the document aim to encourage Member States to establish and maintain appropriate systems and infrastructure for delivering high-quality prosthetics and orthotics services. Implementation depends on the financial, human, and other resources available in each country. While some countries may face greater challenges in implementation, the standards serve as goals to be achieved and benchmarks for resource mobilization. Member States are expected to take gradual steps toward full implementation. Effective implementation requires collaboration among all relevant national stakeholders, including users and their representatives, government ministries, service providers, non-governmental and professional organizations, and donor agencies. The implementation process is suggested to follow four steps: 1. Compare national prosthetics and orthotics systems and services with the complete set of standards to establish a baseline for monitoring future developments. 2. Identify priorities for action, guided by the document's recommendations. 3. Develop a 5–10-year national strategic plan with clear benchmarks for implementation in areas such as policy, products, personnel, and service provision. 4. Conduct annual and mid-term evaluations to assess progress against benchmarks and update the plan as needed. The story of Jaya and Jay from India illustrates the transformative impact of high-quality orthoses. In 1980, Jaya and Jay, aged 5 and 3, respectively, contracted polio, resulting in paralysis of their legs and spines. Despite societal stigma and financial challenges, their parents ensured they received an education. Initially attending a school for children with disabilities, they later transitioned to a regular school, where they faced attitudinal and physical barriers. With determination, family support, and the use of metal orthoses, they completed their schooling. In 1997, Jaya received lightweight plastic orthoses from Mobility India, marking a significant improvement in her quality of life. She was also offered a job as a secretary at Mobility India. Jay followed a similar path, receiving new orthoses and employment. Both siblings married and now have families of their own. Their story highlights the profound difference that access to good-quality orthoses can make, transforming societal attitudes and restoring happiness to their family. The document will be disseminated to a wide network of stakeholders, including WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, WHO collaborating partners, non-governmental and international organizations, professional and research networks, other United Nations agencies, donor agencies, and organizations representing people with disabilities. Dissemination will also occur through ISPO and USAID networks, including their national member societies and country offices. Summaries of the document will be published in relevant journals, and media initiatives will promote its content. The standards proposed in this document are expected to remain valid until 2022. WHO departments responsible for Essential Medicines and Health Products and the Management of Noncommunicable Diseases, Disability, Violence, and Injury Prevention will initiate a review of the standards at that time. However, if significant changes in the evidence base occur within the next five years, an earlier review will be conducted. Prostheses and orthoses are externally applied devices designed to assist individuals with physical impairments or functional limitations, enabling them to lead healthy, productive, independent, and dignified lives. A prosthesis replaces a missing or deficient limb segment, such as an artificial leg or arm. An orthosis supports or modifies the structural and functional characteristics of the neuromuscular and skeletal systems, such as braces or splints. These devices serve various purposes, including improving mobility, alleviating pain, restoring cosmesis, protecting joints, preventing or correcting deformities, and preventing secondary impairments. Most prostheses and orthoses are required for long-term use, while others are needed for limited periods. Prosthetic and orthotic products are classified as health products within healthcare regulations. They are also considered mobility devices, which include wheelchairs and walking aids. Mobility devices, in turn, fall under the broader category of assistive products, which encompass devices for improving vision, hearing, communication, cognition, and environmental interaction. Prosthetics and orthotics is a specialized field within medical and healthcare disciplines, focusing on the research, development, design, manufacture, and application of these devices. The term prosthetics and orthotics encompasses the science, technology, education, and application of these devices. Prosthetics and orthotics services involve a combination of inputs, such as policy, products, and personnel, to deliver appropriate devices and related therapy. These services provide comprehensive care, including preventive, promotive, assistive, and rehabilitative interventions. They typically involve assessing potential users, developing treatment plans, and designing, manufacturing, fitting, and delivering prostheses and orthoses. Prosthetics and orthotics services are integral to healthcare and are often included in rehabilitation services. Their goal is to optimize users' health and well-being. Timely provision of these services is crucial for restoring function and preventing secondary deformities. Combined with other interventions, such as education, skills training, job coaching, and social support, these services contribute to optimal functioning and full participation in society. Users of prosthetics and orthotics services include individuals with physical impairments or functional limitations due to various conditions, such as noncommunicable diseases (e.g., diabetes, stroke, cancer), communicable diseases (e.g., polio, tuberculosis), injuries, degenerative changes, congenital anomalies, or cerebral palsy. Most users have long-term chronic health conditions, requiring lifelong care, including prosthetics and orthotics. Others may need mediumor short-term provision, depending on their condition. Many users require a continuum of care that evolves over their lifetime, necessitating periodic repair, adjustment, modification, and replacement of devices. For example, a 10-year-old child with a lower limb amputation may require 25–30 prostheses over their lifetime. Continuity of care with the same clinician is essential for addressing the complex psychosocial, physical, and technical aspects of the provider-user relationship.
